_comment: One line per symbol. Wording follows EN 1993-1-4:2025 clause 3.2 where the standard defines the symbol. 'symbol' is the exact text used in the calculation trace; 'topics' say which website pages show it. 'detail' is the long explanation for the Help page; 'diagram' names the sketch drawn beside it (csm_curve, plate, section, base_curve, tension, compression, bending).

symbols.name: Yield strength
symbols.meaning: The 0.2 % proof strength: the stress where the steel starts to yield; an input.
symbols.detail: Stainless steel has no sharp yield point, so f_y is the 0.2 % proof strength: the stress that leaves 0.2 % permanent strain after unloading. It is the stress where the first, steep line of the curve ends and the curve starts to round over. Everything in the CSM is measured against it: the strain axis is scaled by ε_y = f_y / E and slenderness is √(f_y / σ_cr). Take it from the material certificate or Table 5.1, not from the grade name alone.

symbols.name: Ultimate tensile strength
symbols.meaning: The highest stress the steel reaches before it fails; an input.
symbols.detail: f_u is the peak of the engineering stress-strain curve. For stainless steel it is far above f_y, and that gap is the whole reason the CSM exists: the classic method stops at f_y and throws the gap away, the CSM lets a stocky section use part of it. The ratio f_y/f_u also controls the ultimate strain ε_u (Formula B.5) and the hardening slope E_sh, so a wrong f_u changes the whole curve.

symbols.name: Average strengths of cold-formed sections
symbols.meaning: Yield and ultimate strength raised by cold-forming; may replace f_y and f_u (B.3(3)); an input.
symbols.detail: Cold-forming (press braking, rolling, drawing) hardens the corners and sometimes the flats of a section, raising its strength above the plain sheet values. B.3(3) allows the raised values f_ya and f_ua to replace f_y and f_u when they are known. In this tool they are simply typed in as custom values; they are not computed here.

symbols.name: Modulus of elasticity
symbols.meaning: Stiffness of the elastic range, the slope of the first line; an input.
symbols.detail: E is the slope of the first line: how much stress per unit of strain before yielding. It sets the yield strain ε_y = f_y / E, and it also appears in the plate and tube buckling stresses (Formulas B.9 and B.11). The standard defines it outside Annex B, so it is an input, never a hidden default.

symbols.name: Poisson's ratio
symbols.meaning: Ratio of lateral to axial strain in the elastic range; an input.
symbols.detail: Poisson's ratio describes how much a plate or wall shrinks sideways when it is squeezed or stretched along its length. It enters the plate buckling stress (B.9) and the tube buckling stress (B.11) through 1 − ν². It is only needed when the engine has to compute σ_cr,cs; if you type σ_cr,cs yourself, ν is not used.

symbols.name: Yield strain
symbols.meaning: Elastic strain at the yield strength, f_y / E.
symbols.detail: ε_y = f_y / E is where the curve leaves the elastic line. It is the natural unit of strain in the CSM: limits are quoted as multiples of it (ε_csm/ε_y, C₁ε_u/ε_y, 15). A section with ε_csm/ε_y = 1 only just reaches yield; above 1 it is using strain hardening.

symbols.name: Ultimate strain
symbols.meaning: Strain at the ultimate strength, estimated from f_y / f_u (Formula B.5).
symbols.detail: ε_u = C₃ (1 − f_y/f_u) (Formula B.5) is an estimate of the strain at ultimate strength. It is estimated from the strength ratio because that is what a designer always has; the actual measured value would need a tensile test. The CSM's two key strains, C₁ε_u and C₂ε_u, are both multiples of it. The larger the gap between f_u and f_y, the more ductile the model assumes the steel to be.

symbols.name: Strain hardening modulus
symbols.meaning: Slope of the second line of the bilinear model: rise over run from (ε_y, f_y) to (C₂ε_u, f_u).
symbols.detail: E_sh is the slope of the second line: how much stress is gained per unit of extra strain once the steel is past yield. It is far smaller than E but not zero, which is exactly the difference from the classic elastic-plastic model (flat after yield, E_sh = 0). It is the rise (f_u − f_y) over the run (C₂ε_u − ε_y). A large E_sh means a lot of strength is available from hardening.

symbols.name: CSM coefficient C1
symbols.meaning: Sets the ductility cap C₁ε_u (Table B.1).
symbols.detail: C₁ comes from Table B.1 and depends on the material family (austenitic, duplex, ferritic and so on). It scales ε_u to give the ductility cap C₁ε_u: the largest strain the CSM lets any member use, however stocky. It protects against relying on strains the material may not safely reach.

symbols.name: CSM coefficient C2
symbols.meaning: Sets where the hardening line ends, C₂ε_u (Table B.1).
symbols.detail: C₂ comes from Table B.1. It places the end of the bilinear curve at C₂ε_u, the strain where the straight hardening line reaches f_u. It is an anchor of the model, not a prediction of fracture.

symbols.name: CSM coefficient C3
symbols.meaning: Scales the ultimate strain ε_u; lower for the less ductile ferritic steels (Table B.1).
symbols.detail: C₃ comes from Table B.1 and sets the size of ε_u = C₃(1 − f_y/f_u). Ferritic steels have a lower C₃ because they are less ductile, so their curve ends sooner and the CSM gives them less credit for strain hardening.

symbols.name: Ductility cap
symbols.meaning: The largest strain the method lets you use.
symbols.detail: C₁ε_u is the upper limit of the strain you may use, set by material ductility alone. In compression B.6/B.7 it caps the stocky branch together with Ω; in tension B.14 compares it with the fixed 15ε_y and uses the smaller. On the chart it is the marker where the hardening line is cut off for design.

symbols.name: End of the bilinear curve
symbols.meaning: Strain where the stress reaches f_u: an anchor point for the straight line, not the fracture strain.
symbols.detail: C₂ε_u is the last point of the bilinear model, where the stress equals f_u. It lies beyond C₁ε_u, so the design never uses the very end of the curve. Do not read it as the failure strain.

symbols.name: Stress at the ductility cap
symbols.meaning: Stress on the hardening line at C₁ε_u.
symbols.detail: This is the height of the hardening line at the ductility cap: f_y + E_sh (C₁ε_u − ε_y). When C₁ε_u governs in tension, this is the design stress f_csm,t. It normally lies between f_y and f_u.

symbols.name: Hardening ratio
symbols.meaning: Hardening slope as a fraction of the elastic slope.
symbols.detail: The hardening ratio compares the second slope with the first. A small value means a very flat second line, so the CSM adds little strength; a larger value means more. It is a quick way to see how much a given material benefits from strain hardening.

symbols.name: Ductility cap ratio
symbols.meaning: The ductility cap as a multiple of the yield strain; compared with 15 in Formula B.14.
symbols.detail: This is the ductility cap in units of yield strain, and it is the quantity that meets the fixed number 15 in Formula B.14. If it is below 15 the material's own ductility governs tension; if it is above 15 the fixed limit of 15 governs. In compression it is compared with Ω.

symbols.name: Plate buckling stress
symbols.meaning: Elastic critical buckling stress of one plate element (Formula B.9).
symbols.detail: σ_cr,p is the stress at which a flat plate under compression would buckle if the steel stayed elastic, k_σ π² E t² / (12 (1 − ν²) b̄²). It depends only on geometry (width b̄, thickness t), edge support (through k_σ) and elastic constants, not on f_y. A wide, thin plate buckles at a low stress.

symbols.name: Section buckling stress
symbols.meaning: Elastic critical local buckling stress of the full cross-section; here the most slender plate.
symbols.detail: σ_cr,cs is the elastic local buckling stress of the whole cross-section. In this tool it is conservatively taken as the lowest σ_cr,p of the plates, which is the most slender plate, because that plate buckles first and drags the section with it. You may also type a value from your own analysis.

symbols.name: Tube buckling stress
symbols.meaning: Elastic critical local buckling stress of a circular hollow section (Formula B.11).
symbols.detail: σ_cr,c is the elastic local buckling stress of a circular hollow section wall, E / √(3(1 − ν²)) × 2t/d (Formula B.11). It rises as the wall gets thicker relative to the diameter. Because tubes buckle in a different mode from flat plates, they have their own formula and their own base curve.

symbols.name: Plate slenderness
symbols.meaning: Relative slenderness of one plate, the square root of f_y / σ_cr,p.
symbols.detail: λ_p = √(f_y / σ_cr,p) compares yield strength with elastic buckling strength for one plate. Below about 1 the plate would reach yield before it buckles; above 1 it buckles first. It is the plate's slenderness: low means stocky, high means slender.

symbols.name: Cross-section slenderness (plates)
symbols.meaning: Relative slenderness of a section of flat plates: the square root of f_y / σ_cr,cs (Formula B.8).
symbols.detail: λ_p,cs = √(f_y / σ_cr,cs) is the slenderness of the whole flat-plate section (Formula B.8). It is the number you read along the horizontal axis of the base curve B.6. Same idea as λ_p, but for the section as a whole.

symbols.name: Cross-section slenderness (tube)
symbols.meaning: Relative slenderness of a circular hollow section: the square root of f_y / σ_cr,c (Formula B.10).
symbols.detail: λ_c,cs = √(f_y / σ_cr,c) is the slenderness of a circular hollow section (Formula B.10). It is the number you read along the horizontal axis of base curve B.7, whose allowed range is much narrower than for plates.

symbols.name: Cross-section slenderness
symbols.meaning: The slenderness used on the base curve: λ_p,cs for plates or λ_c,cs for tubes.
symbols.detail: λ_cs is simply whichever slenderness applies: λ_p,cs for plated sections or λ_c,cs for tubes. It is the horizontal coordinate of the section's point on the base curve and decides the zone: stocky, slender or not allowed.

symbols.name: Plate buckling factor
symbols.meaning: How easily a plate buckles; an input for each plate, and a separate input for bending.
symbols.detail: k_σ is the plate buckling factor. It captures how the plate's edges are held (simply supported, fixed, free, one edge free) and how the stress varies across it. A well-supported plate has a high k_σ and buckles later. Compression and bending load the plates with different stress patterns (a web in pure bending is held back less than one in uniform compression), so a section has one k_σ per plate for compression and another for bending. The standard refers to it from B.5.2(3) but defines it elsewhere (EN 1993-1-5, 6.4.1), so every k_σ is an input.

symbols.name: CSM strain limit
symbols.meaning: The limiting compressive strain the cross-section can reach before local buckling.
symbols.detail: ε_csm is the largest compressive strain the cross-section can reach before local buckling stops it. The CSM uses it as the strain to read the design stress from. A stocky section can reach several times ε_y; a slender one only about ε_y or less.

symbols.name: Strain limit ratio
symbols.meaning: The CSM strain limit as a multiple of the yield strain; above 1 the section can strain-harden.
symbols.detail: This is the value read from the base curve, already capped on the stocky side. A value of 1 means the section reaches yield but no more; greater than 1 means it can use strain hardening, which is where the CSM gains strength over the classic method.

symbols.name: Base curve value
symbols.meaning: The value read from the base curve (B.6 or B.7) before the cap is applied.
symbols.detail: The raw value from Formula B.6 (flat plates) or B.7 (tubes) before the cap is applied. On the stocky branch it rises steeply as slenderness drops, so a cap is required; on the slender branch no cap is needed.

symbols.name: Strain cap
symbols.meaning: The cap on the stocky branch: the smaller of Ω and the material ductility cap.
symbols.detail: The cap on the stocky branch of B.6 and B.7: whichever is smaller of the plastic deformation limit Ω and the material ductility limit C₁ε_u/ε_y. The result shows which one governed, so you can see whether the section or the material is the limit.

symbols.name: Plastic deformation parameter
symbols.meaning: Limit on the permitted plastic strain; an input.
symbols.detail: Ω sets how much plastic strain the designer is willing to allow for the section. It is not defined inside the Annex B formulas, so it is an input. A lower Ω is more conservative. It only matters when it is smaller than the material limit C₁ε_u/ε_y.

symbols.name: Flat plate width
symbols.meaning: Width of the flat part of a plate element; an input.
symbols.detail: b̄ is the flat part of the plate, between the corner radii or welds, not the full outer width. Using the outer width makes the plate look more stocky than it is. It enters σ_cr,p squared in the denominator, so it has a strong effect.

symbols.name: Thickness
symbols.meaning: Thickness of a plate or wall; an input.
symbols.detail: t is the thickness of a plate or tube wall. It enters the buckling stress squared (B.9) or linearly (B.11), so a small increase in t makes a section noticeably less slender.

symbols.name: Outer diameter
symbols.meaning: Outer diameter of a circular hollow section; an input.
symbols.detail: d is the outer diameter of a circular hollow section. The ratio t/d, not either alone, controls the tube's buckling stress. The wall must be thinner than half the diameter.

symbols.name: Web flat width
symbols.meaning: Flat width of the web, an internal plate, from the section dimensions as 8.2.2(5) and Tables 7.2 to 7.4 draw it.
symbols.detail: c_w is the flat part of the web between the fillet toes of a rolled section or the weld toes of a welded one (I-section and channel: h minus two flanges minus two corners), or h minus 3t for the web of a rectangular hollow section. It is the plate width b̄ that Formula B.9 uses for the web, derived by the engine from the dimensions you typed.

symbols.name: Flange flat width
symbols.meaning: Flat width of the flange outstand (or the flange of a rectangular hollow section), derived from the section dimensions per 8.2.2(5).
symbols.detail: c_f is the flat part of the flange: the outstand from the fillet or weld toe to the free edge for an I-section, channel or T-section, or b minus 3t for the flange of a rectangular hollow section. It is the plate width b̄ that Formula B.9 uses for the flange, derived by the engine from the dimensions you typed.

symbols.name: Stem flat width
symbols.meaning: Flat width of the T-section stem outstand: an input, because no table in the standard draws it.
symbols.detail: The tables of the standard draw the flat width of a flange and of a web, but not of the stem of a T-section, so c_stem is typed. It is the plate width b̄ that Formula B.9 uses for the stem; the engine does not derive it. The value must be less than the overall height h.

symbols.name: Cross-sectional area
symbols.meaning: Gross area of the cross-section; an input.
symbols.detail: A is the gross cross-sectional area of the member. It converts stress to force in Formulas B.12, B.15 and B.16. The CSM tension route applies to sections without holes, so net area is not used there; B.6.2 for compression has no clause about holes, so A is the area you enter.

symbols.name: Partial factor
symbols.meaning: Safety factor on cross-section resistance; an input.
symbols.detail: γ_M0 is the partial safety factor applied to cross-section resistance. Its value is given by the Eurocode part and the National Annex that apply, not by Annex B, so it is an input. It divides the resistance, so a larger factor gives a lower, more conservative design value.

symbols.name: Tensile strain limit ratio
symbols.meaning: The smaller of 15 and C₁ε_u/ε_y (Formula B.14).
symbols.detail: Formula B.14: the smaller of the fixed number 15 and the material's own C₁ε_u/ε_y. The result tells you whether the fixed limit or the material ductility is holding back the tensile strain. It is the horizontal position of the design point on the stress-strain curve.

symbols.name: Tensile strain limit
symbols.meaning: Maximum attainable CSM tensile strain.
symbols.detail: The actual tensile strain used for design: the ratio ε_csm,t/ε_y times ε_y. It is the strain at which the design stress is read from the hardening line.

symbols.name: Fixed strain cap
symbols.meaning: The fixed limit of 15 times the yield strain written into Formula B.14.
symbols.detail: The fixed limit written into B.14. It caps the tensile strain the CSM may use, even for a very ductile steel, so that C₁ε_u alone cannot make the strain limit unbounded. It is a rule of the standard, not a material property; the working shows whether this limit or C₁ε_u/ε_y governed.

symbols.name: CSM tensile design stress
symbols.meaning: Stress on the hardening line at ε_csm,t (Formula B.13).
symbols.detail: Formula B.13: the stress on the hardening line at the tensile strain limit, f_y + E_sh ε_y (ε_csm,t/ε_y − 1). It is higher than f_y whenever the strain limit exceeds ε_y, which is the extra strength the CSM adds over the classic method.

symbols.name: CSM tension resistance
symbols.meaning: Design value of the CSM resistance to tension axial force (Formula B.12).
symbols.detail: Formula B.12: A f_csm,t / γ_M0. This is the design resistance of the member in pure tension according to the CSM. It is a resistance only; comparing it with an applied force is left to you because load combinations are outside Annex B.

symbols.name: Branch test
symbols.meaning: Compares ε_csm/ε_y with 1.0 to pick the formula: B.15 or B.16 in compression, B.19 or B.20 in bending.
symbols.detail: Each resistance has a formula for the section that buckles before it yields and one for the section that can strain-harden. Below ε_csm/ε_y = 1.0 the yield resistance is scaled by the ratio (B.15 in compression, B.19 in bending). From 1.0 the hardening is used: B.16 with the stress f_csm of B.17 in compression, B.20 in bending. The two formulas of each pair give the same value at exactly 1.0, so the resistance has no jump.

symbols.name: CSM compressive design stress
symbols.meaning: Stress on the hardening line at ε_csm (Formula B.17); used only when ε_csm/ε_y is at least 1.0.
symbols.detail: Formula B.17: f_y + E_sh ε_y (ε_csm/ε_y − 1), the stress on the hardening line at the strain limit ε_csm of the cross-section. It is defined only from ε_csm/ε_y = 1.0. Below that, Formula B.15 is used and f_csm does not appear.

symbols.name: CSM compression resistance
symbols.meaning: Design value of the CSM resistance of the cross-section to compression axial force (Formulas B.15 and B.16).
symbols.detail: Formula B.15 for ε_csm/ε_y below 1.0, B.16 from 1.0: A times a stress, divided by γ_M0. This is the cross-section resistance only; member buckling (8.3) is outside Annex B, and comparing it with an applied force is left to you.

symbols.name: RHS outer corner radius
symbols.meaning: Outer corner radius of a rectangular hollow section; an input, 0 for sharp corners.
symbols.detail: r_o is the radius of the outer corners of a rectangular hollow section; the inner radius is taken as the larger of r_o − t and 0. It changes the section properties and the drawing only. It does not change the flat width c, which 8.2.2(5) fixes as c = h − 3t. Leave it out and the Deformation and Compression results still appear; only the section properties wait for it.

symbols.name: Centroid, horizontal
symbols.meaning: Horizontal position of the centroid from the lower left corner of the bounding box.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The centroid is the centre of area. Its position is measured from the lower left corner of the box that holds the section, y to the right and z up. It is found by integrating the outline (Green's theorem). It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Centroid, vertical
symbols.meaning: Vertical position of the centroid from the lower left corner of the bounding box.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The centroid is the centre of area. Its position is measured from the lower left corner of the box that holds the section, y to the right and z up. It is found by integrating the outline (Green's theorem). It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Centroid to the top fibre
symbols.meaning: Distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre at the top.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The distance from the centroid to the farthest point of the section on that side. The elastic modulus on that side is I divided by this distance. When the two sides differ, the smaller elastic modulus is the one at the farther fibre. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Centroid to the bottom fibre
symbols.meaning: Distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre at the bottom.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The distance from the centroid to the farthest point of the section on that side. The elastic modulus on that side is I divided by this distance. When the two sides differ, the smaller elastic modulus is the one at the farther fibre. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Centroid to the left fibre
symbols.meaning: Distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre on the left.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The distance from the centroid to the farthest point of the section on that side. The elastic modulus on that side is I divided by this distance. When the two sides differ, the smaller elastic modulus is the one at the farther fibre. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Centroid to the right fibre
symbols.meaning: Distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre on the right.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The distance from the centroid to the farthest point of the section on that side. The elastic modulus on that side is I divided by this distance. When the two sides differ, the smaller elastic modulus is the one at the farther fibre. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Second moment of area about y-y
symbols.meaning: Second moment of area about the horizontal axis through the centroid (the major axis of most sections).
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: I_y is the integral of z² over the area, with z measured from the horizontal axis through the centroid. It measures how stiff the section is against bending about y-y. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Second moment of area about z-z
symbols.meaning: Second moment of area about the vertical axis through the centroid (the minor axis of most sections).
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: I_z is the integral of y² over the area, with y measured from the vertical axis through the centroid. It measures how stiff the section is against bending about z-z. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Product of inertia
symbols.meaning: Product of inertia about the centroid; zero when a symmetry axis exists, and shown for angles.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: I_yz is the integral of y times z over the area, about the centroid. It is zero for a section with an axis of symmetry. For an angle it is not zero, which is why the principal axes are tilted from the legs. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Elastic section modulus about y-y
symbols.meaning: Second moment I_y divided by the distance to the extreme fibre; the smaller of the two sides is the one listed.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: W_el,y is I_y divided by the distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre. When the fibres at the top and the bottom are at different distances (T-sections, angles) there are two values and the smaller is the one to use for first yield. Annex B takes W_el as an input; this value is only a reference. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Elastic section modulus about z-z
symbols.meaning: Second moment I_z divided by the distance to the extreme fibre; the smaller of the two sides is the one listed.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: W_el,z is I_z divided by the distance from the centroid to the extreme fibre. When the fibres on the left and the right are at different distances (channels, angles) there are two values and the smaller is the one to use for first yield. Annex B takes W_el as an input; this value is only a reference. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Plastic neutral axis for y-y
symbols.meaning: Height of the line parallel to y that cuts the area into two equal halves, from the lowest point.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The plastic neutral axis is where the whole section is fully yielded and the compression area equals the tension area, so it cuts the area in half. For bending about y-y it is a horizontal line; its height is measured from the lowest point of the section. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Plastic neutral axis for z-z
symbols.meaning: Distance from the leftmost point to the line parallel to z that cuts the area into two equal halves.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The plastic neutral axis is where the whole section is fully yielded and the compression area equals the tension area, so it cuts the area in half. For bending about z-z it is a vertical line; its distance is measured from the leftmost point of the section. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Plastic section modulus about y-y
symbols.meaning: First moment of the area about the plastic neutral axis for y-y: the bending resistance per unit yield stress when fully yielded.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: W_pl,y is the sum of the first moments of the two halves of the section about the equal-area axis. Multiplied by the yield stress it gives the fully plastic moment. Annex B takes W_pl as an input (Formula B.20); this value is only a reference. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Plastic section modulus about z-z
symbols.meaning: First moment of the area about the plastic neutral axis for z-z: the bending resistance per unit yield stress when fully yielded.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: W_pl,z is the sum of the first moments of the two halves of the section about the equal-area axis. Multiplied by the yield stress it gives the fully plastic moment. Annex B takes W_pl as an input (Formula B.20); this value is only a reference. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Shear centre, horizontal
symbols.meaning: Horizontal position of the shear centre from the lower left corner; a thin-walled approximation.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: The shear centre is the point through which a load must act to bend the section without twisting it. The value here is the thin-walled approximation: the centroid for doubly symmetric sections, where the centrelines of the two legs meet for a T-section or an angle, and e = 3b'²t_f / (6b't_f + h't_w) from the web centreline for a channel. It is an estimate, not an exact value. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Shear centre, vertical
symbols.meaning: Vertical position of the shear centre from the lower left corner; a thin-walled approximation.

symbols.name: Major principal axis angle
symbols.meaning: Angle of the major principal axis u of an angle section from the y axis, counter-clockwise with z up.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: An angle has no axis of symmetry unless its legs are equal, so the axes about which the second moment is largest and smallest (u and v) are tilted from the legs. θ_u gives the direction of the major axis u, measured counter-clockwise from the y axis with z up. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Second moment about the major axis
symbols.meaning: Largest second moment of area of an angle, about the major principal axis u.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: I_u is the largest second moment of area about any axis through the centroid. For an angle it is larger than I_y and I_z, because the legs are tilted from the axes. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Second moment about the minor axis
symbols.meaning: Smallest second moment of area of an angle, about the minor principal axis v.
symbols.clause: geometry, not a rule of EN 1993-1-4
symbols.detail: I_v is the smallest second moment of area about any axis through the centroid. For an angle it is smaller than I_y and I_z, because the legs are tilted from the axes. It is a reference value computed from the dimensions you typed; it enters no calculation unless you click Use in the section geometry window, which copies it into its input field.

symbols.name: Elastic section modulus
symbols.meaning: Section modulus up to first yield, about the axis of bending; an input.
symbols.detail: W_el is the second moment of area about the axis of bending divided by the distance to the outermost fibre: the moment per unit of yield stress at which the extreme fibre first yields. B.6.3.2 names it but gives no way to find it, so it is an input. Take it from the section table, or from the Section geometry window with the Use button. B.19 scales the resistance by it; B.20 uses it through the ratio W_el/W_pl and the hardening term.

symbols.name: Plastic section modulus
symbols.meaning: Section modulus of the fully plastic section, about the axis of bending; an input.
symbols.detail: W_pl is the sum of the first moments of the area above and below the plastic neutral axis, which splits the area in two equal halves. The ratio W_pl/W_el is the shape factor. B.6.3.2 names it but gives no way to find it, so it is an input. Take it from the section table, or from the Section geometry window with the Use button. It sets the size of the plastic reserve in Formula B.20 and is not used by B.19.

symbols.name: Relative slenderness for lateral-torsional buckling
symbols.meaning: How much lateral-torsional buckling limits the beam; decides whether B.6.3 applies; an input.
symbols.detail: λ_LT comes from member design (8.3), which is outside Annex B, so it is an input. B.6.3.1 uses it as a gate. Up to 0.2 the cross-section formulas B.19 and B.20 apply. Between 0.2 and 0.4, Formula B.18 interpolates towards the 8.2.4 resistance (this tool does that in a later phase). Above 0.4, B.6.3 does not apply and the resistance of 8.2.4 is used.

symbols.name: CSM bending parameter
symbols.meaning: The exponent in Formula B.20 that sets how fast the plastic reserve is reached; read from Table B.2.
symbols.detail: α is looked up in Table B.2 from the section type, the axis of bending and, for channels and T-sections, the aspect ratio h/b. It is the exponent of ε_csm/ε_y in the last term of B.20. A larger α makes that term fall faster, so the plastic reserve between W_el and W_pl is used sooner. B.19 does not use it. It is in the PDF, so it is looked up, not typed.

symbols.name: Elastic moment
symbols.meaning: W_el f_y / γ_M0, the moment at first yield; a reference line, equal to Formula B.19 at ε_csm/ε_y = 1.0.
symbols.detail: M_el = W_el f_y / γ_M0 is not a result of Annex B but the value both formulas pass through: B.19 reaches it at ε_csm/ε_y = 1.0, where B.20 starts. It is drawn as a line on the moment chart so you can see where the section is held below first yield (a slender section) and where it goes beyond.

symbols.name: Plastic moment
symbols.meaning: W_pl f_y / γ_M0, the factor in front of the bracket of Formula B.20; a reference line.
symbols.detail: M_pl = W_pl f_y / γ_M0 is the factor in front of the bracket of Formula B.20. With no strain hardening the bracket would tend to 1 and the resistance to M_pl; with hardening the CSM resistance of a stocky section can lie above it. It is drawn as a line on the moment chart. It is not a result of Annex B.

symbols.name: CSM bending resistance
symbols.meaning: Design value of the CSM bending moment resistance of the cross-section about an axis of symmetry.
symbols.detail: Formula B.19 for ε_csm/ε_y below 1.0, Formula B.20 from 1.0. Both start from the strain limit ε_csm of B.5.1, found for the section in bending, and divide by γ_M0. This is the cross-section resistance only: lateral-torsional buckling and the member are outside Annex B, and comparing it with an applied moment is left to you.
